CHAPTER 11 - CONGRUENCE OF TRIANGLES

Introduction

In everyday life we constantly compare shapes. Two postage stamps of the same design, two 5-rupee coins, the two halves of a symmetric butterfly, or two copies of a page printed from the same file all look "exactly the same". In geometry we make this idea precise with the word CONGRUENT. Two figures are said to be congruent if they have exactly the same shape and the same size, so that one can be placed on top of the other and they cover each other completely. This chapter studies congruence for the most basic straight-sided figure - the triangle - and develops simple, reliable tests (called criteria) that tell us when two triangles must be congruent without having to check every part.

11.1 CONGRUENT FIGURES

If one figure can be moved (by sliding, turning, or flipping) so that it fits exactly over another figure, the two figures are congruent. The symbol for congruence is a combination of the "equals" sign with a "tilde" on top; in plain text we write "is congruent to". Congruent figures have equal areas and equal perimeters, but the converse is not true: two figures can have equal areas without being congruent (a 2 by 6 rectangle and a 3 by 4 rectangle both have area 12 but are not congruent). Congruence is a stronger statement than "equal area" - it means every measurement matches.

Examples of congruent figures: two line segments are congruent when they have the same length; two angles are congruent when they have the same measure; two circles are congruent when they have the same radius; two squares are congruent when they have the same side.

11.2 CONGRUENT TRIANGLES AND CORRESPONDENCE OF VERTICES

A triangle has three sides and three angles - six parts in all. Two triangles are congruent when their three pairs of sides and three pairs of angles match exactly. When we write triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR, the ORDER of the letters is important because it tells us the CORRESPONDENCE of vertices:
   A corresponds to P, B corresponds to Q, C corresponds to R.
From this correspondence the matching (corresponding) parts are read off directly:
   Sides: AB = PQ, BC = QR, CA = RP.
   Angles: angle A = angle P, angle B = angle Q, angle C = angle R.
Because the correspondence is built into the order of the letters, writing triangle ABC is congruent to triangle QRP would mean something different (A matches Q, B matches R, C matches P). Always list the vertices so that corresponding vertices occupy the same position in the two names.

11.3 THE NEED FOR CONGRUENCE CRITERIA

To prove two triangles congruent directly we would have to show that all six pairs of parts are equal - three sides and three angles. Fortunately this is far more work than necessary. It turns out that if certain SETS OF THREE parts match, the remaining three are forced to match automatically, and the triangles must be congruent. These minimal sets are the CONGRUENCE CRITERIA. There are four criteria for general triangles - SSS, SAS, ASA and AAS - and one special criterion, RHS, for right-angled triangles.

11.4 SSS (SIDE-SIDE-SIDE) CRITERION

If the three sides of one triangle are equal to the three corresponding sides of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent. In symbols: if in triangle ABC and triangle PQR we have AB = PQ, BC = QR and CA = RP, then triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR. Three side lengths fix a triangle's shape completely - this is exactly why a triangle made of three rigid rods is a rigid, non-collapsing structure, while a four-rod quadrilateral can be flexed. Engineers use triangular bracing in bridges, cranes and roof trusses for precisely this reason.

11.5 SAS (SIDE-ANGLE-SIDE) CRITERION

If two sides and the ANGLE BETWEEN THEM (the included angle) of one triangle are equal to the two corresponding sides and the included angle of another triangle, then the triangles are congruent. In symbols: if AB = PQ, angle A = angle P and AC = PR, then triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR. The key word is INCLUDED: the equal angle must lie between the two equal sides. If the equal angle is not the included angle, the criterion does not apply (see SSA below).

11.6 ASA AND AAS CRITERIA

ASA (ANGLE-SIDE-ANGLE): If two angles and the INCLUDED SIDE (the side between them) of one triangle are equal to the two corresponding angles and the included side of another triangle, then the triangles are congruent. In symbols: if angle B = angle Q, BC = QR and angle C = angle R, then triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR.

AAS (ANGLE-ANGLE-SIDE): If two angles and a NON-included side of one triangle equal the two corresponding angles and the corresponding non-included side of another triangle, the triangles are congruent. AAS follows from ASA: once two angles are known, the third angle is determined by the angle-sum property (the three angles of a triangle add to 180°), so a non-included side can always be converted into an included one. Thus knowing two angles and ANY one side is enough.

11.7 RHS (RIGHT ANGLE-HYPOTENUSE-SIDE) CRITERION

This criterion applies only to RIGHT-ANGLED triangles. If in two right triangles the HYPOTENUSE and one SIDE (leg) of one triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and the corresponding side of the other, then the triangles are congruent. In symbols: if angle B = angle Q = 90°, the hypotenuses AC = PR and one leg BC = QR, then triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR. RHS works because, by the Pythagoras theorem, once the hypotenuse and one leg are fixed the third side is determined, which effectively reduces RHS to an SSS argument.

11.8 WHY SSA AND AAA ARE NOT CRITERIA

Not every set of three matching parts guarantees congruence.

SSA (two sides and a NON-included angle) fails: given two sides and an angle that is not between them, two genuinely different triangles can often be built. This is the well-known "ambiguous case". For example, with a fixed angle at A and a fixed side AB, a second side of a given length swung from B can meet the opposite ray in two different points, producing two non-congruent triangles. (The only time SSA does force congruence is when the angle is a right angle or obtuse, or the fixed side is long enough - and the right-angle version is exactly the RHS criterion.)

AAA (all three angles equal) fails: equal angles guarantee the same SHAPE but not the same SIZE. Two equilateral triangles, one with side 2 cm and one with side 5 cm, have all angles 60° but are clearly not congruent - one is larger than the other. Triangles with equal angles are called SIMILAR, not congruent. Congruence needs at least one pair of equal sides to fix the size.

11.9 CPCT - CORRESPONDING PARTS OF CONGRUENT TRIANGLES

Once two triangles have been proved congruent by one of the criteria, ALL their corresponding parts are equal. This principle is abbreviated CPCT (Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are equal), sometimes written CPCTC. CPCT is the workhorse of geometric proof: we prove a congruence using three parts, and then use CPCT to deduce the equality of the OTHER parts (the remaining sides or angles) that we actually wanted. For instance, to prove that two segments are equal, we often show they are corresponding sides of a pair of congruent triangles and then quote CPCT.

11.10 PROPERTIES OF ISOSCELES TRIANGLES

An ISOSCELES triangle has two equal sides. The angles opposite these equal sides have a beautiful and useful property.

Isosceles Triangle Theorem: In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal. That is, if in triangle ABC we have AB = AC, then angle B = angle C (the base angles are equal).
Proof (using SAS and CPCT): Draw AD, the bisector of angle A, meeting BC at D. In triangle ABD and triangle ACD: AB = AC (given), angle BAD = angle CAD (AD bisects angle A), and AD = AD (common). By SAS, triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD. Hence by CPCT, angle B = angle C.

Converse: If two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite them are equal (so the triangle is isosceles). That is, if angle B = angle C then AB = AC. This means "equal sides <-> equal opposite angles" works in both directions.

A useful corollary: the median from the apex (top vertex) of an isosceles triangle, the bisector of the apex angle, and the perpendicular from the apex to the base all coincide with the SAME line - the axis of symmetry - and this line bisects the base at right angles. An EQUILATERAL triangle (all three sides equal) is isosceles in three ways, so all three of its angles are equal; since they add to 180°, each equals 60°.

11.11 SIMPLE APPLICATIONS AND WORKED PROOFS

Congruence turns "seeing" into "proving". A few standard results:
 - The diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into two congruent triangles (by ASA or SAS), which is why opposite sides and opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.
 - A point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is equidistant from its endpoints (prove the two right triangles congruent by SAS, then CPCT).
 - A point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from the two arms of the angle (RHS + CPCT).
 - In surveying, the width of a river or the distance across an inaccessible gap can be found by constructing a congruent triangle on accessible ground and measuring the matching side.

Worked example: In triangle ABC, AB = AC and D is the midpoint of BC. Prove that AD is perpendicular to BC. In triangle ABD and triangle ACD: AB = AC (given), BD = CD (D is midpoint), AD = AD (common). By SSS, triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD. By CPCT, angle ADB = angle ADC. But angle ADB + angle ADC = 180° (angles on a straight line BC), so each is 90°. Hence AD is perpendicular to BC.

SUMMARY

- Two figures are congruent if they have the same shape and size, so one exactly covers the other; congruent figures have equal areas and perimeters, but equal area alone does not imply congruence.
- Congruent triangles have all six parts (three sides, three angles) equal. The order of letters in triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR fixes the correspondence of vertices and hence of parts.
- Four criteria prove congruence of general triangles: SSS (three sides), SAS (two sides and the included angle), ASA (two angles and the included side) and AAS (two angles and a non-included side).
- RHS proves congruence of right triangles from the hypotenuse and one leg.
- SSA and AAA are NOT valid criteria: SSA is ambiguous, and AAA gives similar (same-shape) but not necessarily congruent triangles.
- CPCT: once triangles are proved congruent, all remaining corresponding parts are equal - this is used to deduce further equalities in proofs.
- Isosceles triangle: angles opposite equal sides are equal, and conversely equal angles force equal opposite sides; an equilateral triangle has all angles 60°.

topics.name: Congruent Figures and Triangles
topics.description: Meaning of congruence (same shape and size, exact superposition); congruence of segments, angles and circles; congruent triangles and the correspondence of vertices read from the order of letters in the congruence statement.

topics.name: SSS and SAS Criteria
topics.description: The Side-Side-Side criterion (three pairs of equal sides) and the Side-Angle-Side criterion (two sides and the included angle); the meaning of 'included angle' and the rigidity of triangles; why SSA is not a valid criterion.

topics.name: ASA and AAS Criteria
topics.description: The Angle-Side-Angle criterion (two angles and the included side) and the Angle-Angle-Side criterion (two angles and a non-included side); how AAS reduces to ASA using the angle-sum property; why AAA is not a valid criterion.

topics.name: RHS Criterion
topics.description: The Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side criterion for right triangles; equality of hypotenuse and one leg forces congruence; its link to the Pythagoras theorem and to the special SSA case.

topics.name: CPCT and Applications
topics.description: Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Equal; using a proved congruence to deduce equality of remaining sides and angles; standard applications such as parallelogram diagonals, perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors.

topics.name: Isosceles Triangle Properties
topics.description: Angles opposite equal sides are equal and its converse; the apex bisector/median/altitude coincide as the axis of symmetry; equilateral triangles have all angles equal to 60°.

learning_outcomes.description: Explain the meaning of congruent figures and congruent triangles and read the correspondence of vertices, sides and angles from a congruence statement.
Apply the SSS and SAS criteria to test or prove the congruence of two triangles, identifying the included angle in SAS.
Explain, with counterexamples, why SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) does not guarantee congruence.
Apply the ASA and AAS criteria to prove congruence and explain how AAS follows from ASA using the angle-sum property; explain why AAA fails.
Apply the RHS criterion to prove congruence of right-angled triangles from the hypotenuse and one leg.
Use CPCT to deduce equality of remaining corresponding parts after proving a congruence, and apply this in geometric and real-life problems.
State and use the isosceles triangle theorem (angles opposite equal sides are equal) and its converse.
Prove properties of isosceles and equilateral triangles using congruence criteria and CPCT.

chapter_summary.title: Congruence of Triangles - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This chapter makes the idea of two shapes being 'exactly the same' precise through congruence. It focuses on triangles: what it means for two triangles to be congruent, the shortcut criteria (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, RHS) that prove congruence without checking all six parts, why SSA and AAA fail, the CPCT principle, and the properties of isosceles triangles.

sections.heading: Congruent figures and triangles
bullets: Two figures are congruent if they have the same shape and size, so that one placed on the other covers it completely.
Congruent figures have equal areas and perimeters, but equal area alone does NOT make figures congruent (a 2x6 and a 3x4 rectangle both have area 12).
In triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR, the order of letters gives the correspondence: A<->P, B<->Q, C<->R, so AB=PQ, BC=QR, CA=RP and angle A=angle P, etc.

sections.heading: SSS and SAS criteria
bullets: SSS: if the three sides of one triangle equal the three corresponding sides of another, the triangles are congruent.
SAS: if two sides and the INCLUDED angle (the angle between those sides) match, the triangles are congruent.
The included angle is essential; using a non-included angle gives SSA, which is not a valid criterion.
Three fixed side lengths make a triangle rigid, which is why triangular bracing is used in bridges and trusses.

sections.heading: ASA, AAS and why AAA fails
bullets: ASA: two angles and the INCLUDED side (between the angles) equal implies congruence.
AAS: two angles and a NON-included side equal implies congruence; it follows from ASA because the third angle is fixed by the 180 degree angle sum.
So knowing two angles and any one side is enough to prove congruence.
AAA is NOT a criterion: equal angles give the same shape but not the same size (two equilateral triangles of different sizes) - these triangles are similar, not congruent.

sections.heading: RHS criterion for right triangles
bullets: RHS applies only to right-angled triangles.
If the hypotenuse and one leg of one right triangle equal the hypotenuse and corresponding leg of another, the triangles are congruent.
It works because Pythagoras theorem fixes the third side once the hypotenuse and one leg are known, reducing RHS to SSS.

sections.heading: CPCT and isosceles triangles
bullets: CPCT (Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Equal): after proving congruence with three parts, all remaining corresponding parts are equal.
Isosceles triangle theorem: angles opposite the equal sides are equal (base angles equal); the converse also holds - equal angles force equal opposite sides.
In an isosceles triangle the apex angle bisector, the median to the base and the altitude to the base coincide and bisect the base at right angles.
An equilateral triangle has all sides equal, so all three angles are equal to 60 degrees.

key_takeaways: Congruent means identical in shape AND size - one figure exactly covers the other; equal area alone is not enough.
The order of vertices in a congruence statement encodes which parts correspond.
Valid criteria: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS for any triangle; RHS for right triangles.
SSA is ambiguous and AAA gives only similarity - neither proves congruence.
CPCT lets you deduce the remaining equal parts once a congruence is established.
Isosceles triangle: equal sides give equal opposite (base) angles and vice versa; equilateral triangles have all angles 60 degrees.
Congruence converts visual 'sameness' into rigorous proof and underlies many results about parallelograms, bisectors and constructions.

The side lying between two named angles of a triangle; used in the ASA criterion.

If two angles and a non-included side of one triangle equal the corresponding parts of another, the triangles are congruent.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Congruence of Triangles
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Draw rough figures where helpful, quote the congruence criterion (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS or RHS) you use, and justify every deduced equality with CPCT. Show all steps of your proofs.

questions.question: Two triangles are stated to be congruent as triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF. Write down all pairs of equal sides and all pairs of equal angles.
questions.answer:
The order of letters gives the correspondence A<->D, B<->E, C<->F.
Equal sides: AB = DE, BC = EF, CA = FD.
Equal angles: angle A = angle D, angle B = angle E, angle C = angle F.
So all six corresponding parts are equal.
questions.explanation: Read corresponding parts directly from the order of the vertices in the congruence statement.

questions.question: In triangle ABC and triangle DEF, AB = DE = 5 cm, BC = EF = 6 cm and CA = FD = 7 cm. Are the triangles congruent? State the criterion and write the congruence in correct vertex order.
questions.answer:
All three pairs of corresponding sides are equal (AB=DE, BC=EF, CA=FD), so by the SSS criterion the triangles are congruent.
Congruence: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF.
This matches vertices A<->D, B<->E, C<->F.

questions.question: State the SAS criterion and explain, with the meaning of 'included angle', why the equal angle must be the included one.
questions.answer:
SAS: if two sides and the INCLUDED angle of one triangle are equal to the corresponding two sides and included angle of another triangle, the triangles are congruent.
The included angle is the angle lying BETWEEN the two named sides (for sides AB and AC the included angle is angle A). Fixing the two side lengths and the angle between them locks the position of the third vertex, so the triangle is completely determined. If instead the equal angle were opposite one of the sides (a non-included angle), we would have SSA, which can produce two different triangles - so congruence is no longer guaranteed.
questions.explanation: Included angle fixes the third vertex; non-included angle gives the ambiguous SSA case.

questions.question: Explain why AAA (all three angles equal) is not a criterion for congruence. Give an example.
questions.answer:
Equal angles guarantee the same SHAPE but not the same SIZE. When all three angle pairs are equal the triangles are SIMILAR, meaning one is a scaled copy of the other, but they need not be congruent.
Example: an equilateral triangle of side 2 cm and an equilateral triangle of side 5 cm both have all angles equal to 60 degrees, yet one is clearly larger than the other, so they are not congruent.
To prove congruence at least one pair of equal SIDES is needed to fix the size.
questions.explanation: AAA fixes shape only; two equilateral triangles of different sizes are the standard counterexample.

questions.question: Two right triangles ABC and PQR have right angles at B and Q. Given AC = PR = 13 cm (hypotenuses) and BC = QR = 5 cm. Prove the triangles are congruent and find AB.
questions.answer:
Both triangles are right-angled (angle B = angle Q = 90 degrees). The hypotenuses are equal (AC = PR = 13) and one leg is equal (BC = QR = 5). By the RHS criterion, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR.
To find AB, use Pythagoras in triangle ABC: AB^2 = AC^2 - BC^2 = 13^2 - 5^2 = 169 - 25 = 144, so AB = 12 cm.
By CPCT, PQ = AB = 12 cm as well.
questions.explanation: RHS applies; Pythagoras gives the third side, and CPCT transfers it.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, AB = AC. The bisector of angle A meets BC at D. Prove that (a) triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD, (b) BD = DC, and (c) AD is perpendicular to BC.
questions.answer:
Given: AB = AC and AD bisects angle A, so angle BAD = angle CAD.
(a) In triangle ABD and triangle ACD:
  AB = AC (given),
  angle BAD = angle CAD (AD is the bisector),
  AD = AD (common side).
  By SAS, triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD.
(b) By CPCT, BD = DC. So D is the midpoint of BC.
(c) By CPCT, angle ADB = angle ADC. But B, D, C are collinear, so angle ADB + angle ADC = 180 degrees. Therefore 2 angle ADB = 180, giving angle ADB = 90 degrees. Hence AD is perpendicular to BC.
Thus in an isosceles triangle the bisector of the apex angle is also the median and the altitude to the base.
questions.explanation: SAS gives the congruence; CPCT gives BD=DC and equal adjacent angles that sum to 180, forcing 90 degrees.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, angle B = angle C. Prove that AB = AC (converse of the isosceles triangle theorem), and name the triangle.
questions.answer:
Given angle B = angle C. Draw AD, the bisector of angle A, meeting BC at D, so angle BAD = angle CAD.
In triangle ABD and triangle ACD:
  angle BAD = angle CAD (construction),
  angle B = angle C (given),
  AD = AD (common).
  By AAS, triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD.
By CPCT, AB = AC. Since two sides are equal, triangle ABC is ISOSCELES.
questions.explanation: Use AAS with the angle bisector; CPCT gives AB=AC.

questions.question: In quadrilateral ABCD, AB = CD and AD = CB. Using a diagonal, prove that triangle ABD is congruent to triangle CDB and state one pair of equal angles you obtain.
questions.answer:
Draw diagonal BD. In triangle ABD and triangle CDB:
  AB = CD (given),
  AD = CB (given),
  BD = DB (common diagonal).
  By SSS, triangle ABD is congruent to triangle CDB.
By CPCT, angle A = angle C (and also angle ABD = angle CDB, angle ADB = angle CBD).
The equality angle ADB = angle CBD makes AD parallel to CB, confirming ABCD is a parallelogram.
questions.explanation: SSS on the two triangles formed by a diagonal; CPCT gives equal angles.

questions.question: Give one real-life application of triangle congruence and briefly say how it is used.
questions.answer:
Surveying an inaccessible distance: to find the width of a river without crossing it, a surveyor sets up a triangle on the near bank that is congruent to the triangle spanning the river (by fixing equal angles and an included side, i.e. ASA). Because the triangles are congruent, the accessible side of the constructed triangle equals the river's width by CPCT, so the width is measured on land.
Another example is triangular bracing in bridges and roof trusses: three fixed side lengths (SSS) make a triangle rigid, so the structure cannot deform.
questions.explanation: ASA/CPCT for indirect measurement; SSS rigidity for structures.

questions.question: Explain with a diagram-in-words why SSA does not in general prove congruence.
questions.answer: Take a fixed angle at A and a fixed side AB along one arm. From B swing a second segment of a fixed length so that its far end lands on the other arm of the angle. If that length is shorter than AB but longer than the perpendicular distance from B to the arm, the swung segment meets the arm at TWO different points, say C1 and C2. This gives two triangles, triangle ABC1 and triangle ABC2, which have the same angle at A, the same side AB and the same swung side length - yet they are not congruent (BC1 and BC2 reach different points). Because two different triangles satisfy the same SSA data, SSA cannot guarantee congruence. This is called the ambiguous case.
questions.explanation: A swung side can meet the opposite arm at two points, giving two non-congruent triangles.

questions.explanation: By CPCT angle D = angle A.

questions.question: To measure the width of a river indirectly, one constructs on land a triangle that is ___ to the river-spanning triangle.
questions.explanation: Congruent triangle -> equal matching side = width.

questions.question: The isosceles triangle theorem is usually proved using the criterion
In an equilateral triangle, all angles are equal because it is isosceles with respect to
options: each of its three pairs of sides
questions.answer: each of its three pairs of sides
questions.explanation: Equal in three ways -> all base angles equal.

questions.question: In triangle PQR, PQ=PR. A student concludes angle Q=angle R. This is
questions.explanation: Angles opposite equal sides are equal.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, AB=AC. The perpendicular from A to BC meets BC at D. Then BD is
questions.explanation: Altitude from apex bisects the base (CPCT).

questions.question: In isosceles triangle ABC with AB=AC, the exterior angle at B equals 130 degrees. Then angle A equals
questions.explanation: angle B=50 so angle C=50, angle A=180-100=80.

questions.question: All congruent figures have equal areas.
Two figures with equal areas are always congruent.
questions.explanation: Equal area does not force same shape/size.

questions.question: SSS is a valid criterion for congruence of triangles.
SSA always guarantees that two triangles are congruent.
AAA is sufficient to prove two triangles congruent.
AAS can always be reduced to ASA using the angle-sum property.
questions.explanation: The third angle is determined, converting a non-included side to an included one.

questions.question: The RHS criterion is used only for right-angled triangles.
CPCT is applied only after two triangles are proved congruent.
questions.explanation: It deduces the remaining equal parts.

questions.question: In an isosceles triangle the base angles are equal.
questions.explanation: Angles opposite equal sides are equal.

questions.question: If two angles of a triangle are equal, the triangle must be equilateral.
questions.explanation: It is isosceles; equilateral needs all three equal.

questions.question: Two figures that have the same shape and size are called ______.
If triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR, then side CA corresponds to side ______.
The criterion that uses three pairs of equal sides is ______.
In the SAS criterion, the equal angle must be the ______ angle.
Two sides and a non-included angle equal is the ______ situation, which is not a valid criterion.
In the ASA criterion the equal side is the side ______ the two angles.
Triangles with all three angles equal but different sizes are called ______.
In RHS, besides the right angle, the equal parts are the hypotenuse and one ______.
RHS reduces to SSS because the third side is fixed by the ______ theorem.
The full form of CPCT is Corresponding Parts of Congruent ______ are Equal.
If triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF and BC = 9 cm, then EF = ______ cm.
A triangle with two equal sides is called ______.
In triangle ABC, AB = AC and angle B = 55 degrees; then angle C = ______ degrees.
Each angle of an equilateral triangle measures ______ degrees.
In triangle ABC with AB = AC and angle A = 100 degrees, each base angle = ______ degrees.
Define congruent figures and give two examples.
questions.answer:
Two figures are congruent if they have exactly the same shape and size, so that one placed on the other covers it completely.
Examples: (1) two line segments of the same length; (2) two circles of the same radius. (Also two squares of the same side, or two copies of the same photograph.)

questions.question: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle RQP. List the three pairs of equal sides.
questions.answer:
The order gives A<->R, B<->Q, C<->P.
Equal sides: AB = RQ, BC = QP, CA = PR.
questions.explanation: Read correspondence from the vertex order.

questions.question: Are two triangles of equal area necessarily congruent? Explain with an example.
questions.answer: No. Equal area does not fix shape and size. For example a triangle with base 6 and height 4 has area 12, and a triangle with base 8 and height 3 also has area 12, but their sides and angles differ, so they are not congruent. Congruence requires all corresponding sides and angles to be equal, which is stronger than equal area.
questions.explanation: Equal area is weaker than congruence.

questions.question: How many pairs of equal parts do two congruent triangles have, and what are they?
questions.answer: Six pairs: three pairs of equal sides and three pairs of equal angles. In triangle ABC congruent to triangle PQR these are AB=PQ, BC=QR, CA=RP and angle A=angle P, angle B=angle Q, angle C=angle R.

questions.question: State the SSS congruence criterion.
questions.answer: If the three sides of one triangle are equal to the three corresponding sides of another triangle, then the two triangles are congruent. Symbolically, if AB=PQ, BC=QR and CA=RP then triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR.

questions.question: In triangle ABC and triangle ADC, AB = AD and CB = CD. Prove the two triangles are congruent.
questions.answer:
In triangle ABC and triangle ADC:
  AB = AD (given),
  CB = CD (given),
  AC = AC (common side).
  By SSS, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle ADC.
questions.explanation: SSS with the common side AC.

questions.question: In triangle ABC and triangle PQR, AB = PQ = 5 cm, angle A = angle P = 60 degrees and AC = PR = 7 cm. Prove congruence and state which parts become equal.
questions.answer:
In triangle ABC and triangle PQR:
  AB = PQ = 5 cm (given),
  angle A = angle P = 60 degrees (included angle),
  AC = PR = 7 cm (given).
  By SAS, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR.
By CPCT the remaining parts are equal: BC = QR, angle B = angle Q and angle C = angle R.

questions.question: Explain the difference between SAS and SSA, and state which one is a valid criterion.
questions.answer:
In SAS the equal angle is the INCLUDED angle - it lies between the two equal sides. Fixing two sides and the angle between them determines the third vertex uniquely, so SAS is a VALID criterion.
In SSA the equal angle is NON-included - it is opposite one of the two sides. Here the third vertex may lie at two different positions (the ambiguous case), so two non-congruent triangles can satisfy the same data. Hence SSA is NOT a valid criterion.
The only exception is when the non-included angle is a right angle, which is exactly the RHS criterion.

questions.question: Give a clear reason, with an example, why SSA fails to guarantee congruence.
questions.answer:
SSA fixes two sides and an angle NOT between them. Swinging the second side from its endpoint, its far end can land on the opposite ray at two distinct points, producing two triangles with the same two side lengths and the same angle but different shapes.
Example: take angle A = 30 degrees, AB = 8 cm, and a side of length 5 cm swung from B. The 5 cm side meets the other arm at two points, giving two different triangles ABC1 and ABC2 that are not congruent. Because two triangles fit the same SSA data, SSA cannot prove congruence.

questions.question: A student writes: 'In triangle ABC and triangle DEF, AB = DE, BC = EF and angle A = angle D, therefore the triangles are congruent by SAS.' Identify and correct the error.
questions.answer: The error is calling this SAS. In SAS the equal angle must be INCLUDED between the two equal sides. Here the equal sides are AB and BC (whose included angle is angle B, not angle A); the given equal angle A is opposite BC, so the data is actually SSA - two sides and a non-included angle. SSA does not guarantee congruence. To fix the argument we would need either the included angle (angle B = angle E) for SAS, or the third side (CA = FD) for SSS.
questions.explanation: Given data is SSA, not SAS.

questions.question: State the ASA and AAS criteria.
questions.answer:
ASA: if two angles and the INCLUDED side (the side between them) of one triangle are equal to the corresponding two angles and included side of another, the triangles are congruent.
AAS: if two angles and a NON-included side of one triangle equal the corresponding parts of another, the triangles are congruent.

questions.question: Explain how AAS can be derived from ASA.
questions.answer: Suppose in two triangles two angles and a non-included side are equal (AAS). Since the sum of the three angles of any triangle is 180 degrees, once two angles are equal the third angles are also equal. Now in each triangle the equal 'non-included' side becomes the side included between one of the original equal angles and the newly found equal third angle. Thus the AAS data is converted into ASA data (two angles and the included side), and ASA proves the congruence. Therefore AAS is valid because it reduces to ASA.
questions.explanation: Third angle fixed by 180 -> converts to ASA.

questions.question: Why does knowing all three angles (AAA) fail to prove congruence, while knowing two angles and one side succeeds?
questions.answer: AAA fixes only the SHAPE of a triangle - all triangles with the same three angles are similar (scaled copies) and can have any size, so they need not be congruent (e.g. equilateral triangles of side 2 cm and 5 cm). Knowing two angles and one side adds SIZE information: the single equal side pins down the scale, and with two equal angles the third is fixed by the angle sum, so the whole triangle is determined (ASA or AAS). Hence two angles plus one side is enough, but three angles alone is not.
questions.explanation: One side fixes size; AAA fixes only shape.

questions.question: In triangle ABC and triangle DEF, angle B = angle E, angle C = angle F and BC = EF. Prove congruence and deduce that AB = DE.
questions.answer:
In triangle ABC and triangle DEF:
  angle B = angle E (given),
  BC = EF (included side, given),
  angle C = angle F (given).
  By ASA, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF.
By CPCT, AB = DE (corresponding sides).

questions.question: State the RHS congruence criterion.
questions.answer: In two RIGHT-angled triangles, if the hypotenuse and one side (leg) of one triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and the corresponding side of the other, then the two triangles are congruent. (RHS = Right angle-Hypotenuse-Side.)

questions.question: In right triangles ABC and DEF, angle B = angle E = 90 degrees, AC = DF = 10 cm and BC = EF = 6 cm. Prove congruence and find AB.
questions.answer:
Both triangles are right-angled at B and E. The hypotenuses are AC = DF = 10 cm and one leg BC = EF = 6 cm are equal. By RHS, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF.
Using Pythagoras in triangle ABC: AB^2 = AC^2 - BC^2 = 100 - 36 = 64, so AB = 8 cm. By CPCT, DE = 8 cm too.

questions.question: Justify why the RHS criterion is valid by relating it to SSS.
questions.answer: In a right triangle the hypotenuse and one leg are given equal in the two triangles. By the Pythagoras theorem the remaining leg is determined: (leg)^2 = (hypotenuse)^2 - (given leg)^2. Since the hypotenuse and the given leg are equal in both triangles, the third sides computed this way are also equal. Now all three pairs of sides are equal, so by SSS the triangles are congruent. Thus RHS is really an SSS argument made possible by Pythagoras, which is why it is restricted to right triangles.

questions.question: What does CPCT mean and when is it used?
questions.answer: CPCT stands for 'Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Equal'. It is used AFTER two triangles have been proved congruent by a criterion (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS or RHS): once congruence is established, every remaining pair of corresponding sides and angles is equal, and CPCT lets us state those equalities.

questions.question: Prove that a point P on the perpendicular bisector of segment AB is equidistant from A and B.
questions.answer:
Let the perpendicular bisector meet AB at M, so AM = MB and angle PMA = angle PMB = 90 degrees.
In triangle PMA and triangle PMB:
  AM = MB (M is the midpoint),
  angle PMA = angle PMB = 90 degrees (perpendicular),
  PM = PM (common).
  By SAS, triangle PMA is congruent to triangle PMB.
By CPCT, PA = PB. Hence P is equidistant from A and B.
questions.explanation: SAS at the foot M, then CPCT gives PA = PB.

questions.question: In a parallelogram ABCD, prove that a diagonal divides it into two congruent triangles.
questions.answer:
Draw diagonal AC. Since ABCD is a parallelogram, AB is parallel to DC and AD is parallel to BC.
In triangle ABC and triangle CDA:
  angle BAC = angle DCA (alternate angles, AB parallel DC),
  AC = CA (common),
  angle BCA = angle DAC (alternate angles, AD parallel BC).
  By ASA, triangle ABC is congruent to triangle CDA.
By CPCT, AB = CD and BC = DA, which is why opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.
questions.explanation: ASA using alternate angles; CPCT gives opposite sides equal.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, AD is drawn so that BD = DC and AB = AC. Prove AD bisects angle A.
questions.answer:
In triangle ABD and triangle ACD:
  AB = AC (given),
  BD = DC (given),
  AD = AD (common).
  By SSS, triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD.
By CPCT, angle BAD = angle CAD, so AD bisects angle A. (By CPCT we also get angle ADB = angle ADC = 90 degrees, showing AD is the perpendicular bisector of BC.)
questions.explanation: SSS then CPCT gives equal angles at A.

questions.question: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR. If AB = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm and CA = 10 cm, find PQ, QR, RP and the perimeter of triangle PQR.
questions.answer:
By CPCT: PQ = AB = 6 cm, QR = BC = 8 cm, RP = CA = 10 cm.
Perimeter of triangle PQR = 6 + 8 + 10 = 24 cm (equal to the perimeter of triangle ABC).

questions.question: State the isosceles triangle theorem and its converse.
questions.answer:
Theorem: In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the equal sides are equal (if AB = AC then angle B = angle C).
Converse: If two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite them are equal (if angle B = angle C then AB = AC), so the triangle is isosceles.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, AB = AC and angle A = 50 degrees. Find angle B and angle C.
questions.answer: Let angle B = angle C = x (base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal). By the angle-sum property, 50 + x + x = 180, so 2x = 130 and x = 65. Therefore angle B = angle C = 65 degrees.

questions.question: In triangle PQR, angle Q = angle R = 70 degrees. Which sides are equal and why? Find angle P.
questions.answer:
Since angle Q = angle R, the sides opposite them are equal (converse of the isosceles theorem): the side opposite angle Q is PR and the side opposite angle R is PQ, so PQ = PR. Thus triangle PQR is isosceles.
angle P = 180 - 70 - 70 = 40 degrees.
questions.explanation: Equal angles -> equal opposite sides; angle P = 40.

questions.question: Prove that the angles opposite the equal sides of an isosceles triangle are equal.
questions.answer:
Let triangle ABC have AB = AC. Draw AD, the bisector of angle A, meeting BC at D, so angle BAD = angle CAD.
In triangle ABD and triangle ACD:
  AB = AC (given),
  angle BAD = angle CAD (AD bisects angle A),
  AD = AD (common).
  By SAS, triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD.
By CPCT, angle ABD = angle ACD, that is angle B = angle C. Hence the base angles are equal.
questions.explanation: SAS via the apex bisector, then CPCT.

questions.question: Prove that each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60 degrees.
questions.answer:
Let triangle ABC be equilateral, so AB = BC = CA.
Since AB = AC, by the isosceles theorem angle B = angle C.
Since BA = BC, by the same theorem angle A = angle C.
Therefore angle A = angle B = angle C. By the angle-sum property their sum is 180 degrees, so 3 (angle A) = 180, giving angle A = angle B = angle C = 60 degrees.
questions.explanation: Isosceles in three ways -> all angles equal -> 60 each.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, AB = AC. The perpendicular from A meets BC at D. Prove BD = DC.
questions.answer:
AD is perpendicular to BC, so angle ADB = angle ADC = 90 degrees.
In right triangles ABD and ACD:
  hypotenuse AB = AC (given),
  AD = AD (common leg),
  angle ADB = angle ADC = 90 degrees.
  By RHS, triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD.
By CPCT, BD = DC. Hence the altitude from the apex bisects the base.
questions.explanation: RHS on the two right triangles, then CPCT.

questions.question: triangle ABC has AB = AC. Is it possible for angle B to be a right angle? Justify.
questions.answer: No. Since AB = AC, the base angles are equal: angle B = angle C. If angle B were 90 degrees, then angle C would also be 90 degrees, and their sum alone would be 180 degrees, leaving 0 degrees for angle A - which is impossible for a genuine triangle. Therefore in an isosceles triangle the two equal base angles must each be less than 90 degrees; only the apex angle can be right or obtuse.
questions.explanation: Two 90-degree base angles would exceed the angle sum.

questions.question: State one everyday situation where the RHS criterion is useful and explain briefly.
questions.answer: Comparing two right-angled ramps or ladders leaning against a wall: each forms a right triangle whose hypotenuse is the ramp/ladder and whose vertical leg is the height reached. If two ladders have the same length (equal hypotenuses) and reach the same height on the wall (equal legs), then by RHS the two right triangles are congruent, so they make the same angle with the ground and their feet are the same distance from the wall (by CPCT).
questions.explanation: Equal hypotenuse and leg in right triangles -> RHS -> equal base and angle.

questions.question: A carpenter builds a wooden bracket in the shape of triangle ABC and wants an identical spare triangle PQR. He measures AB = PQ = 12 cm, BC = QR = 16 cm and CA = RP = 20 cm. (a) Which congruence criterion guarantees the two brackets are identical? (b) Write the congruence statement in correct order. (c) What is the measure relation of angle A and angle P? (d) Why is a triangular bracket rigid?
questions.answer:
(a) All three pairs of sides are equal, so the SSS criterion applies.
(b) triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR (A<->P, B<->Q, C<->R).
(c) By CPCT, angle A = angle P (corresponding angles of congruent triangles).
(d) Three fixed side lengths determine a triangle completely (SSS), so its shape cannot change - a triangle cannot be deformed without changing a side length, which is why triangular frames are rigid.
questions.explanation: SSS congruence, CPCT for angles, rigidity from three fixed sides.

questions.question: Two identical right-angled ramps are built. Each has a vertical support (leg) and a sloping top (hypotenuse). For ramp 1, the slope AC = 25 cm and vertical leg BC = 7 cm, with the right angle at B. For ramp 2, the slope DF = 25 cm and vertical leg EF = 7 cm, right angle at E. (a) Which criterion proves the ramps congruent? (b) State the congruence. (c) Find the horizontal base AB. (d) What is DE?
questions.answer:
(a) Both are right triangles with equal hypotenuses (AC = DF = 25) and one equal leg (BC = EF = 7), so the RHS criterion applies.
(b) triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF.
(c) By Pythagoras, AB^2 = AC^2 - BC^2 = 625 - 49 = 576, so AB = 24 cm.
(d) By CPCT, DE = AB = 24 cm.
questions.explanation: RHS; Pythagoras gives base 24 cm; CPCT transfers it.

questions.question: To find the width of a river, a surveyor stands at point A on one bank directly opposite a tree T on the far bank. She walks along the bank to a peg B, marks the midpoint P of AB, then walks perpendicular to AB away from the river to a point C such that C, P and T are in a straight line. She measures AC. (a) Name the two triangles involved. (b) Which criterion shows they are congruent? (c) Why does AC equal the river width AT? (d) State the principle used to justify (c).
questions.answer:
(a) triangle APT (spanning the river) and triangle BPC (on land). Here AP = PB (P is the midpoint), angle A = angle B = 90 degrees (both perpendicular to the bank line at A and B in this standard set-up), and angle APT = angle BPC (vertically opposite, since C, P, T are collinear).
(b) By ASA, triangle APT is congruent to triangle BPC.
(c) By CPCT, the corresponding sides AT and BC are equal, so measuring BC on land gives the river width AT. (In the simplest layout the measured accessible side equals the required width by this congruence.)
(d) The principle is CPCT - corresponding parts of congruent triangles are equal.
questions.explanation: ASA congruence via midpoint and vertically opposite angles; CPCT gives the width.

questions.question: A triangular road sign is isosceles with AB = AC. The apex angle at A is measured as 40 degrees. (a) What are the base angles angle B and angle C? (b) Which property did you use? (c) If instead angle B were measured as 75 degrees, what would angle C and angle A be? (d) Could this sign ever be equilateral with apex 40 degrees?
questions.answer:
(a) Base angles are equal: angle B = angle C = (180 - 40)/2 = 70 degrees each.
(b) The isosceles triangle theorem - angles opposite equal sides (AB, AC) are equal - together with the angle-sum property (180 degrees).
(c) By the same theorem angle C = angle B = 75 degrees, so angle A = 180 - 75 - 75 = 30 degrees.
(d) No. An equilateral triangle has all angles 60 degrees, so its apex could not be 40 degrees.
questions.explanation: Base angles equal; angle sum; equilateral needs all 60.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, AB = AC. D is the midpoint of BC and AD is joined. (a) Prove triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD. (b) Show AD bisects angle A. (c) Show AD is perpendicular to BC. (d) Name the single line AD represents in the isosceles triangle.
questions.answer:
(a) In triangle ABD and triangle ACD: AB = AC (given), BD = DC (D is midpoint), AD = AD (common). By SSS, triangle ABD is congruent to triangle ACD.
(b) By CPCT, angle BAD = angle CAD, so AD bisects angle A.
(c) By CPCT, angle ADB = angle ADC. Since B, D, C are collinear, angle ADB + angle ADC = 180 degrees, so each is 90 degrees; hence AD is perpendicular to BC.
(d) AD is simultaneously the median to BC, the bisector of angle A and the altitude from A - the axis of symmetry of the isosceles triangle.
questions.explanation: SSS then CPCT; median = bisector = altitude coincide.

questions.question: Two triangular garden plots are laid out. In plot 1, triangle ABC, angle B = 55 degrees, angle C = 65 degrees and BC = 30 m. In plot 2, triangle PQR, angle Q = 55 degrees, angle R = 65 degrees and QR = 30 m. (a) Which criterion shows the plots congruent? (b) Write the congruence. (c) Find angle A and angle P. (d) Are AB and PQ equal? Why?
questions.answer:
(a) Two angles and the included side are equal (angle B = angle Q, BC = QR, angle C = angle R), so the ASA criterion applies.
(b) triangle ABC is congruent to triangle PQR.
(c) angle A = 180 - 55 - 65 = 60 degrees, and by CPCT angle P = angle A = 60 degrees.
(d) Yes, AB = PQ by CPCT, since they are corresponding sides of congruent triangles.
questions.explanation: ASA with included side BC; angle sum; CPCT.

questions.question: A student is given two triangles with AB = DE = 7 cm, BC = EF = 5 cm and angle C = angle F = 40 degrees, and claims they are congruent by SAS. (a) Identify the two sides and the angle given. (b) Is the angle the included angle for these two sides? (c) Which case is this really? (d) Is the conclusion of congruence guaranteed?
questions.answer:
(a) The two equal sides are AB and BC (and DE, EF); the equal angle is angle C (and angle F).
(b) No. The included angle between sides AB and BC is angle B, not angle C. angle C is opposite side AB, so it is a NON-included angle.
(c) This is the SSA case (two sides and a non-included angle).
(d) No, congruence is NOT guaranteed. SSA is the ambiguous case and can be satisfied by two different triangles. The student would need the included angle B (for SAS) or the third side CA (for SSS) to prove congruence.

questions.question: In figure, OA = OB and OC = OD, where the two segments AB and CD cross at O so that A, O, D are collinear and B, O, C are collinear. (a) Which pair of angles at O are equal and why? (b) Prove triangle AOC is congruent to triangle BOD. (c) Deduce AC = BD. (d) What is the relation between lines AC and BD suggested by the equal alternate angles?
questions.answer:
(a) angle AOC = angle BOD because they are vertically opposite angles.
(b) In triangle AOC and triangle BOD: OA = OB (given), angle AOC = angle BOD (vertically opposite), OC = OD (given). By SAS, triangle AOC is congruent to triangle BOD.
(c) By CPCT, AC = BD.
(d) By CPCT, angle CAO = angle DBO; these are equal alternate angles for lines AC and BD with transversal AB, so AC is parallel to BD.
questions.explanation: SAS using vertically opposite angles; CPCT gives AC=BD and parallelism.

questions.question: Two students compare a 5-rupee coin and its photocopy printed at the same size, and separately compare a small square tile of side 10 cm with a large square tile of side 20 cm. (a) Are the coin and its same-size photocopy congruent? (b) Are the two square tiles congruent? (c) Are they at least the same shape? (d) State the difference between 'congruent' and 'same shape'.
questions.answer:
(a) Yes - the coin and a same-size printed copy have identical shape and size, so they are congruent.
(b) No - the tiles have the same shape but different sizes (10 cm vs 20 cm side), so they are not congruent.
(c) Yes, both tiles are squares, so they have the same shape (they are similar).
(d) 'Same shape' (similar) means the figures look alike but may differ in size; 'congruent' is stronger - same shape AND same size, so one exactly covers the other.
questions.explanation: Congruent = same shape and size; similar = same shape only.

questions.question: In figure, AC and BD are two segments that bisect each other at point O (so AO = OC and BO = OD). (a) Which angles at O are equal? (b) Prove triangle AOB is congruent to triangle COD. (c) Deduce AB = CD. (d) Which criterion did you use?
questions.answer:
(a) angle AOB = angle COD (vertically opposite angles).
(b) In triangle AOB and triangle COD: AO = OC (O bisects AC), angle AOB = angle COD (vertically opposite), BO = OD (O bisects BD). Hence the two triangles are congruent.
(c) By CPCT, AB = CD.
(d) The SAS criterion (two sides AO, BO and the included angle at O).
questions.explanation: SAS with vertically opposite included angle; CPCT gives AB=CD.
